title: The Canyon Sample Switch
short: Two habitat specimens seem to have swapped labels during a survey.
brief: A fictional ecology club used Cowiche Canyon as the setting for a survey workshop. Two sealed soil sample jars were labeled as creekside and upland, but their measurements appear reversed. The jars were never taken from any real protected site: this is a fictional classroom dataset. Use particle analysis, habitat clues, and the transfer log to determine how the switch occurred.
caseQuestion: Who changed the sample labels, and which tests reveal the mix-up?

clues.title: Creekside field notes
clues.detail: The creekside note describes a dark, damp mixture containing many fine particles. No protected vegetation is disturbed in this fictional model.
clues.question: Which jar should match creekside notes?

clues.title: Upland field sketch
clues.detail: A sketch shows gritty material on an exposed slope away from the creek. The drawing is descriptive, not a real soil map.
clues.question: What would strengthen an upland assignment?

clues.title: Temporary adhesive tags
clues.detail: The tag marked U appears attached to a backing labeled C. The marker ink is fresh compared with the original archive sheet.
clues.question: What process likely created uncertainty?

clues.title: Jar seal check
clues.detail: Neither seal is broken, and the sample masses match the earlier collection sheet. The contents were likely not poured into different jars.
clues.question: Which distinction matters?
options: A suspect versus a chemical formula

clues.title: Particle sieve readings
clues.detail: Jar 14 contains 62% coarse grains; Jar 29 contains 21%. The original field sheet assigns Jar 14 to the upland station.
clues.question: What does Jar 14 most strongly resemble?

clues.title: Original photo log
clues.detail: Before the labels were rewritten, a photograph shows number 29 beside the creekside worksheet. It also shows 14 beside the upland worksheet.
clues.question: Why is the photograph valuable?

clues.title: Transfer sheet
clues.detail: The transfer sheet has a single signature at the time of relabeling. No second person checked the correspondence between jar numbers and habitat names.
clues.question: What would reduce future switches?

labs.title: Particle comparison
labs.story: Change coarse-particle fraction to model how a sample differs from fine creek material.
labs.explanation: Higher coarse fraction produces a higher texture index in this simplified proxy.
labs.question: Which scientific interpretation is best supported by this model?
options: Higher coarse percentage supports a coarser specimen.
Particle percentage proves a person guilty.
Coarse and fine grains are identical.

labs.title: Water retention
labs.story: Change the fine fraction and compare a modeled water-holding score.
labs.explanation: Fine material can change water retention, but real soil behavior depends on structure and organic matter.
labs.question: Which scientific interpretation is best supported by this model?
options: Particle fraction never affects water properties.
Higher fine fraction can raise this model’s retention.
The index is a real field certification.

labs.title: Label exposure
labs.story: Change elapsed exposure time to estimate a fictitious label readability score.
labs.explanation: The label readability index is illustrative, not a validated ink-aging technique.
labs.question: Which scientific interpretation is best supported by this model?
options: Longer exposure always improves paper tags.
A tag identifies its writer by color.
More exposure decreases readability in this model.

math.prompt: Jar 14 contains 62% coarse particles. If a 200 g model sample has that composition, how many grams are coarse?

explanation: The original photograph and particle measurements preserve the sample identities. The sample cataloger relabeled the containers, and no second verification prevented a name swap.

witnesses.name: Eden Marsh
witnesses.statement: I was helping with the sample inventory after the paper tags got wet. I remember setting both jars on the same desk.
witnesses.followup: Two sticky labels overlapped, and I was working quickly when the group returned.
witnesses.question: Which item can test Eden’s memory of original jar numbers?

witnesses.name: Levi Archer
witnesses.statement: I drew the sample sites from the trail, then returned with the group. I never handled the sealed lids.
witnesses.followup: The creekside site has visibly darker damp ground than the upland site.
witnesses.question: What could corroborate Levi’s habitat description?

witnesses.name: Nina Flores
witnesses.statement: I checked that every sample had a lid and date. I did not inspect new handwriting after lunch.
witnesses.followup: We should have photographed each label before and after transfer.
witnesses.question: What check did Nina not complete?
options: A second hike with new people

witnesses.name: Omar Bell
witnesses.statement: I carried the box to the desk without opening it. One tag was stuck to the other.
witnesses.followup: The paper tags became damp during transport.
witnesses.question: How does Omar’s account relate to the labels?
options: It suggests a possible transport complication
It proves the jar contents were swapped

note: Entirely fictional educational case using a real regional place name as setting. No actual person, facility, business, incident, or allegation is represented.
